newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Emergency over, Russia space probe plunges into sea.
newsitem.headline: Emergency over, Russia space probe plunges into sea.

text.p: Russia's stricken Mars space probe crashed harmlessly into the Pacific Ocean on Monday after sparking a short-lived national emergency thousands of kilometres (miles) away in Australia.

Prime Minister John Howard put the army and civil defence officials on alert after being told by U.S. President Bill Clinton that the Mars-96 probe, carrying four lethal plutonium canisters, could crash in Australia.

An Australian defence official told Reuters the probe, which ran into trouble after blasting off from Kazakhstan on Saturday, tumbled down between Easter Island and Chile at about 0134 GMT after overflying both Australia and New Zealand.
It was not clear how much of the six-tonne craft survived its re-entry into the Earth's atmosphere.

Clinton, due to arrive in Australia on Tuesday on his first overseas trip since his reelection, called Howard early on Monday to warn that U.S. scientists expected the probe to come down over eastern Australia.

The vast majority of this island continent is virtually uninhabited but U.S. officials said the probe or its debris could hit near Canberra, Australia's small, purpose-built political capital in the south-east of the country.
Howard, appealing for calm, told reporters Clinton had not reconsidered his visit in light of the potential emergency.
"He's looking forward to seeing us," Howard said with a laugh. "He's pretty comfortable and relaxed."

But one agoraphobic woman phoned a Sydney radio station to complain that she spent the morning in fear, huddled in a shed at the bottom of the garden, because of the non-stop news coverage generated by the potential emergency.
"What right has the media to make my life a living hell for the last three hours?" the woman asked.
Australia space-tracking equipment could not follow the errant probe and Howard's government had to be kept up to date by U.S. monitoring stations.

Howard said Russian officials had assured the United States and Australia the plutonium battery-canisters, containing a total 200 grams of the radioactive material, were designed to withstand the heat of re-entry into the earth's atmosphere and the impact of a crash.
But he ordered Australia's military and civil defence forces to activate a pre-planned emergency strategy designed to deal with space debris, with teams assembling around the country.
"We want people to know what the situation is, but we don't want people to be melodramatic about it," Howard said.
The head of Emergency Management Australia said nuclear emergency teams stood by as nuclear fallout was considered the greatest danger.

The remote outback town of Tibooburra in New South Wales was near the first predicted crash site and local publican Alan Lowe said residents became very excited when they heard the town mentioned on the radio news.
Soon afterwards, however, word came from the United States that the probe would end up somewhere in the Pacific and Lowe decided to offer free drinks all round.
"We are one relieved town," he said.
